# A Parallel Smith-Waterman Algorithm Based on Divide and Conquer $^{*}$

$\mathrm{F a Z H A N G}^{1},$ Xiang-Zhen QIAO $^{1}$ and Zhi-Yong LIU $^{2}$

1 Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100080,

{zf, qiao }@ncic.ac.cn

2 National Natural Science Foundation of China, Beijing, 100083, zliu@rose.nsfc.gov.cn

## Abstract

Biological sequence comparison is an important tool for researchers in molecular biology. There are several algorithms for sequence comparison. The Smith-Waterman algorithm, based on dynamic programming, is one of the most fundamental algorithms in bioinformatics. However the existing parallel Smith-Waterman algorithm needs large memory space. As the data of biological sequences expand rapidly, the memory requirement of the existing parallel Smith-Waterman algorithm has becoming a critical problem. For resolving this problem, we develop a new parallel Smith-Waterman algorithm using the method of divide and conquer, named PSW-DC. Memory space required in the new parallel algorithm is reduced significantly in comparison with existing ones. A key technique, named The C&E method, is developed for the implementation of the new parallel Smith-Waterman algorithm.

Keywords: biological sequence alignment, dynamic programming, divide and conquer, parallel

## 1. Introduction

The nearly exponential growth rate of biological sequence database threatens to overwhelm existing computational methods for biological data analysis and

searching. The computational demand needed to explore and analyze the data contained in these databases is quickly becoming a great concern. To meet these demands, we must use high performance computing systems, such as parallel computers.

Biological sequences can be treated as strings over a fixed alphabet of characters, a,c,t and g. An alignment is a way of stacking one sequence above the other and matching characters from the two sequences that lie in the same position [1]. From the alignment, we can find two subsequences contained respectively in two sequences that have the most similarity. The problem of the biological sequence alignment is the most faced in the exploring and analyzing the data, no matter in sequence assembly, comparison of homology, finding of gene coding region and prediction of protein's structure and function [2].

There are several methods for alignment of two biological sequences. The dynamic programming is probably the most popular programming method in sequences alignment [3]. The Needleman-Wunsch algorithm, the first algorithm applying the dynamic programming to comparing biological sequences, was proposed by Needleman and Wunsch in 1970[5]. Later, Smith and Waterman improved the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm and proposed the well-known Smith-Waterman algorithm [6]. The time complexity of these algorithm is $O(mn)$ ,where m,n are the lengths of the two sequences respectively. Because the cores of these algorithms are

dynamic programming, all algorithms need to manipulate an $( n+1 ) \times( m+1 )$ matrix, named dynamic programming matrix.

The most time spent in these algorithms is calculating the dynamic programming matrix, so research work on parallelization of two sequences alignment focuses mostly on the calculation of the matrix. Edmiston et al. [7] presented parallel algorithms for sequence and subsequence matching that can use up to $O(\min(m,n))$ processors. Lander [8] discussed implementation on CM2, a data parallel computer. Galper and Brutlag [9] presented two different parallel Smith-Waterman methods, Row Wavefront method and Diagonal Wavefront method. About the research of dynamic programming, Qiao et al. [10] summarized the pipeline, backward diagonal and blocked backward diagonal parallel strategies. However, in order to obtain the optimal result, these algorithms need to store the entire dynamic programming matrix in each parallel processor. As the growth of biological sequence database, the length of sequences often becomes very long, and the size of the matrix becomes very large. Thus, not only the execution time of these algorithms needs to be very long, the memory space needed in the algorithm becomes very large. Even in some cases the size of the matrix is bigger than the size of memory space in one processor.

In this paper, we present a parallel Smith-Waterman algorithm using the method of divide and conquer, named PSW-DC algorithm. According to our algorithm, each processor needs only to store a matrix, whose size is $1 / p$ that of the entire dynamic programming matrix, where p is the number of the processors in a parallel system. Compared with existing algorithm, the memory space requirement is largely reduced. Thus, each processor only generates an intermediate result. How to obtain the final result from intermediate results becomes a critical problem of the PSW-DC algorithm. So, a key technique, named the C&E method, for combine the intermediate results is developed.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In section 2 we review the Smith-Waterman algorithm. In

section 3 we present the PSW-DC algorithm and the C&E method. In section 4, we give the implementation and experimental results of the parallel Smith-Waterman algorithm on DAWNING 2000-I cluster system. We conclude the paper in section 5.

## 2.1 Biological Sequence Alignment

Biological sequence alignment, viz. sequence similarity comparison, is likely the most frequently performed task in bioinformatics. Because of the mutations in the lengthy course of evolution, the wrong base was incorporated instead of the true copy. So in many applications two sequences may not be highly similar as a whole, but may contain regions that are highly similar.

To describe the sequence similarity, let us first define the following basic terminology [1,2,4].

Scoring function: Let $\sum$ be the alphabet, ( for DNA, we take $\Sigma=\{A,C,G,T\}$ , the four bases, and for proteins we take $\Sigma$ to be the 20 amino acids.) a special symbol, '-', denotes a space, which means an insertion or deletion caused by mutation. The scoring function $f$ : $\sum \cup\{‘-’\} \times$ $\Sigma \cup\{‘-’\} \rightarrow R$ prescribes the score for any position in the alignment, that is if x and y are characters in $\Sigma$ or space, then $f(x,y)$ denotes the score of aligning x and y. In general, if x and y are matching, the score is a positive otherwise, the score is zero or a negative.

Gap: A gap is any maximal sequence of consecutive space in a single sequence of a given alignment. The length of the gap is the number of space in it, denoted as #spaces. The number of gaps in the alignment is denoted as #gaps.

For example, consider the following alignment:

$$
S ^ {\prime} = a t t c - - g a - t g g a c c
$$

$$
T ^ {\prime} = a - - c g t g a t t - - - c c

This alignment has four gaps containing a total of eight spaces, #gaps is four, and #space is two, one, two

and three, respectively.

Gap helps create alignments that better conform to underlying biological models and more closely fit patterns that one expects to find in meaningful alignment. However, each gap has a corresponding penalty weight model. A generalized penalty model is the affine gap weight model, $W_{g} + W_{s}\times(\# spaces)$ ,where $W_{g}$ represents the penalty of initiating a gap, and $W_{s}$ represents the penalty of extending the gap by one space.

Alignment: Let S and T be strings. An alignment A maps S and T into strings $S^{\prime}$ and $T^{\prime}$ that may contain space characters, where

1. $| S^{\prime} |=| T^{\prime}|$ , (where $| S^{\prime} |$ and $| T^{\prime} |$ denote the length of $S^{\prime}$ and $T^{\prime}$ , respectively) and

2. The removal of spaces from $S^{\prime}$ and $T^{\prime}$ (without changing the order of the remaining characters) leaves S and T, respectively.

Optimal alignment: An optimal alignment of S and T is one that has the maximum possible value for these two strings. An optimal local alignment can be described by finding the subsequences $\alpha$ and $\beta$ of S and T respectively, whose similarity is the maximum over all such pairs of subsequences.

The algorithm consists of two parts: calculation of the total score indicating the similarity between the two given sequences, and identification of the optimal alignment by tracing back the path that lead to the score.

Analyzing equation (2), we can find the relation of data dependence in dynamic programming (Figure 2): the value of $D(i,j)$ depends on the value of $D(i-1,j-1),D(i-1,j)$ and $D(i,j-1).$ Because of the data dependence, many algorithms, such as those found in [1,7,8,9,10], were designed to allow parallel manipulation of the edit matrix. However these algorithms need large communication latency between the processors in cluster computer systems, and need to store the entire edit matrix in every processor. As the volume of biological sequences

database expanding, the memory space requirement in cluster computer systems becomes critical.

## 3. A New Parallel Smith-Waterman Algorithm -- PSW-DC

For resolving the critical requirement of memory space, we present a coarse grain parallel method for Smith-Waterman algorithm, using the strategy of divide and conquer, named PSW-DC. This algorithm can significantly reduce the memory space that the general parallel Smith-Waterman algorithm required.

## 3.1 The PSW-DC Algorithm

The basic idea of the PSW-DC algorithm is as follows. Firstly, the original data is partitioned according to the number of processors and distributed to every processor. Secondly the Smith-Waterman algorithm is executed independently on each processor. Thirdly, the intermediate results of each processor are combined and the optimal local alignment is obtained.

In practice, an unknown sequence usually needs to compare with several known sequences in a sequence database. Often the unknown sequence is called as query sequence and the known sequence is named as subject sequence.

In practice, an unknown sequence usually needs to compare with several known sequences in a sequence database. Often the unknown sequence is called as query sequence and the known sequence is named as subject sequence.

Let query sequence be S, subject sequence be T, and the number of processors in a parallel system be p. According to the method, firstly we divide the query sequence S into p subsequences, described as $S_{0}, S_{1}, \dots,$ $S_{p-1}$ , and the length of each subsequence is $\frac{\left|S\right|}{p}$ ; then allocate the query subsequence $S_{i}$ to the processor $P_{i}$ where 0 $\leq i < p$ , and at the same time broadcast the entire subject sequence T to all of the processors; and then, run the Smith-Waterman algorithm for query subsequence $S_{i}$ and subject sequence T in processor $P_{i}$ independently, and get a local result $A_{i}$ in processor $P_{i}$ ; finally, manipulate all of the local result $A_{i}$ and obtain the final result A of query sequence S and subject sequence T.

From Figure 3, we can find that each processor $P_{i}$ only needs to store an $\left( \frac{\mid S\mid}{p}+1\right)\times\left(\mid T\mid+1\right)$ edit matrix $D_{i}$ in the new Smith-Waterman algorithm. Thus, a new problem has arisen: how to obtain the final result A of query sequence S and subject sequence T from the intermediate result $A_{i}$ in each processor?

## 3.2 The C&E (Combine and Extend) Method

We present the C&E (combine and extend) method to resolve the above problem. For simplicity, we explain the C&E method for the case of $p=2$ . Suppose that the query sequence S is divided into subsequences $S_{0}$ and $S_{1}$ and the intermediate results on the two processors $P_{0}$ and $P_{1}$ are $A_{0}$ and $A_{1}$ respectively. There are only six relations between $A_{0}$ and $A_{1}$ as shown from Figure 4a to Figure 4f in Figure 4.

Suppose that the tail of $A_{0}$ is E, corresponding to the entry $(i_{0}, j_{0})$ in the edit matrix $D_{0}$ . E represents that the last column of $A_{0}$ consists of the $i_{0}$ th character of $S_{0}$ and the $j_{0}$ th character of T. H, the head of $A_{1}$ , corresponds to the entry $(i_{1}, j_{1})$ in the edit matrix $D_{1}$ , and represents that the first column of the $A_{1}$ consists of the $i_{1}$ th character of $S_{1}$ and the $j_{1}$ th character of T.

Figure 4a shows that $A_{0}$ consists of a subsequence of $S_{0}$ and a subsequence that lies in the tail of T, while $A_{1}$ consists of a subsequence of $S_{1}$ and a subsequence of T that lies in the beginning of T. That is $j_{0}=|T|$ and $j_{1}=1.$

In Figure 5, we can see that E, the tail of $A_{0}$ has arrived at the tail of sequence T, whereas, H, the head of $A_{1}$ has reached the head of sequence T. That is $A_{0}$ cannot extend downwards, and $A_{1}$ cannot extend upwards either. So in this case, we consider that the result A is the local alignment, whose score is max $(M_{0}, M_{1})$

Figure 4b shows that $E$ , the tail of $A_{0}$ has arrived at the tail of sequence $T$ , and the head of $A_{1}$ , H, doesn't arrived at the head of sequence $T$ . So $A_{0}$ cannot extend downwards, but $A_{1}$ can extend upwards, that is $j_{0}=|T|$ and $j_{1}>1$ . In this case, we need to extend the alignment $A_{1}$ using the algorithm of retracement. In the extending process some mismatch and gaps will be generated, which will reduce the score of $A_{1}$ . In order that the extending process will not reduce the score of $A_{1}$ severely, we set up a threshold $\theta$ such that if the score of $A_{1}$ is less than $\theta$ , we will not make such an extension. If $A_{1}$ is extended to the top of edit matrix $D_{1}$ , and $j_{1}>1$ , which means that $A_{1}$ doesn't extend to the head of $T$ , then we transfer the message of the new head of $A_{1}$ to processor $P_{0}$ , and continue extending $A_{1}$ in edit matrix $D_{0}$ . Suppose that the last result of $A_{1}$ is $A_{1}^{\prime}$ , its score is $M_{1}^{\prime}$ , then $M_{1}^{\prime}$ must higher than $M_{1}$ . The final result $A$ is the local alignment, whose score is $\max \left( M_{0}, M_{1}^{\prime} \right)$ .

Figure 4c shows that $A_{1}$ cannot extend upwards, but $A_{0}$ can extend downwards. Here we need to extend $A_{0}$ downwards using the backward retrace method. We also set up a threshold $\theta$ like Figure 4b. If $A_{0}$ is extended to the bottom of the edit matrix $D_{0}$ , we need to transfer the message of the new tail of $A_{0}$ to processor $P_{1}$ , continue extending $A_{0}$ in edit matrix $D_{1}$ . Suppose that the last result of $A_{0}$ is $A_{0}^{\prime}$ , its score is $M_{0}^{\prime}$ , and $M_{0}^{\prime}$ must higher than $M_{0}$ . The final result A is the local alignment, whose score is max $(M_{0}^{\prime}, M_{1})$

## 4. Implementation and Experiment Results

We have implemented the PSW-DC algorithm on a

cluster system named DAWNING 2000-I. All programs are written in C, and the message passing communication between processors is done by MPI.

For testing the sensitivity and the speedup of result, we generated query and subject sequences of varying lengths, and ran with 1,2,4,8 and 16 processors. Sensitivity results and run-time results are shown in Table 1 and Table 2, speedup results are shown in Figure 6.

The figures in the table are the similarity percentage of results in several processors compared with the results in one processor. for the same sequence pair, as the increment of processors, the length of query subsequences assigned to each processor will be shortening, and that decreases the sensitivity of results. For the same number of processors, as the increment of

the length of sequences pairs, the sensitivity of results will increase.

In biology, the category and function of a query sequence is decided not only by the result of sequences alignments, but also by the protein's 3-D structure of the sequence. So the results of the sequence alignment are only regarded as a reference, and some discrepancy is allowed. At present, there is no existing widely accepted measure of the range of discrepancy in sequences alignments, because of the complicated biological mechanism. A prevailing opinion is that an algorithm is feasible if it makes much improvement in run-time at the cost of losing little sensitivity.

## 5. Conclusion

In this paper we present a new parallel Smith-Waterman algorithm for sequences alignments using the technique of divide and conquer and implement the algorithm in a cluster system. In our algorithm, the original sequence data is partitioned and distributed to every processor. An intermediate result is generated in each processor. We also present the C&E method to obtain the final result from the intermediate result in each processor, when only a part of the edit matrix is stored in each processor.

Our algorithm significantly reduces the memory space that the existing algorithms required. In the existing algorithms, we need to store an $( n+1 ) \times( m+1 )$ matrix in each processor. When the size of the matrix is bigger than the size of the total memory space of each processor, the data cannot to be handled according to the old algorithm. In comparison, in our algorithm, each processor needs to store a part of the edit matrix, and needs only $1/p$ that of the matrix in existing algorithms, where p is the number of processors. So, the data, not to be handled in existing algorithms, can easily be handled using our algorithm.
